name: Kira Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for St Brigid's Home Support, a charity in our seaside town that does end-of-life care in people's own homes. Some days it's personal care, washing and turning someone who's very ill, and some nights I do a sit, staying awake beside someone so their family can sleep. I've done it six years. I grew up helping look after my grandmother, so it came naturally.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: What I like is being trusted at the hardest time a family has. What wears me out is the nights, and the funerals, because I go to more than I should. The night sits pay extra, so I earn more than most carers, and my parents helped me and my partner Daniel buy our flat, so we're settled. The worry is St Brigid's money, because it lost a council grant last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So it's like the internet fridges, everyone talks about it and then nobody bothers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and that good care was never something a computer could do. With Daniel's mates down the pub I'd laugh about it. Online I'd keep quiet, I don't like arguing with strangers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, AI was never my worry. St Brigid's losing that grant is my worry. If the charity cuts night sits, I lose the shifts that make my wage decent, and that's got nothing to do with robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at St Brigid's and ask for every night sit going. I'd also take a couple of private night sits a month for families from church who've asked me before, paid on top. And I'd keep saving what I can, just in case the charity shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm about AI. Uneasy about the charity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How likely is it that St Brigid's cuts the night sits?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say half and half. We've been told the money runs out in spring unless a new donor comes. My manager Sister Margaret has fought for us, but she can't pay us in prayers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Private sits for church families. Tell me more about how that works.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A family I know from Mass asked me last year to sit with their dad privately. I did three nights, they paid me directly, and it felt right. I'd do that more if the charity cut back.

I'd **keep quiet online**, because I don't argue with strangers.
think: AI was never my worry; the **lost council grant** is.
If night sits go, I lose the shifts that make my **wage decent**.
do: Ask for **every night sit** going at the charity.
Take a couple of **private night sits** a month for church families.
Keep **saving** in case the charity shrinks.
feel: **Calm about AI**, uneasy about the charity's money.
S0.quote: My manager Sister Margaret has fought for us, but she can't pay us in prayers.
fieldNote: Her pressure is **charity funding**, not technology.
Her **church network** already gives her private work on the side.
She'd stay loyal to a manager who's been **honest** about money.

steps.text: Ask the charity for every night sit on the rota
Take two private night sits a month for church families

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the paperwork world changes and we carry on mostly. I can see that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no app for holding someone's hand when they're dying. At work I'd say let's see what the new systems actually do before we moan. At Mass people would ask, and I'd tell them their nurses and carers aren't going anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it might even help St Brigid's. If AI does the funding applications and the rota, Sister Margaret could spend less on office staff and more on night sits. My job's the hands-on bit, so I'd be fine for a long while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the sits and the personal care. Once the other carers had used the care notes app for a few months, I'd learn it too, because I don't like being first. I've used a chatbot before to help word a sympathy card, so I'm not scared of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit hopeful about the charity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said AI might help the charity save on office staff. How would that feel for the office staff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not nice, I know. Moira in the office has been there twenty years and she'd probably go. I'd feel guilty being glad about it, but more sits means more families helped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the sympathy card.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lady I'd sat with for weeks died, and I didn't know what to write to her daughter. I asked the chatbot for ideas, then wrote my own words in my own hand. It was a help, but the card had to come from me.

say: I'd say there's **no app** for holding a dying person's hand.
I'd tell colleagues to see what the **new systems** do before moaning.
think: AI doing **funding applications** could free money for night sits.
My **hands-on job** would be fine for a long while.
do: Keep doing the **sits and personal care**.
Learn the **care notes app** after others have used it.
Use a chatbot for **wording**, but write cards in my own hand.
feel: **Calm**, and a bit hopeful about the charity.
S1.quote: There's no app for holding someone's hand when they're dying.
fieldNote: She sees AI as a possible **rescue** for the charity's tight budget.
She feels **guilty** that savings might cost an office colleague her job.
She uses AI for help but keeps **personal words** her own.

steps.text: Keep doing the night sits and personal care rounds
Learn the care notes app after colleagues have used it a few months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. And robots by 2031. That's very quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there are some things you don't hand to a machine, and dying is one of them. I'd say it at church and to anyone who asked. I'd probably sign something if the parish started a petition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think palliative care would be one of the last bits to go, but the basic care around it, the washing and turning, could go by 2031. If St Brigid's can get a robot to do the nights for less, the charity would have to, with money that tight. Daniel's plumbing would be under threat around then too, which scares me more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build up my private families from church, so if the charity goes, I've got my own clients who want a person. I'd save harder, both of us, maybe half of Daniel's earnings for a year. And honestly, we'd probably marry and try for a baby sooner, while we're both still earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like the floor's tilting a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your work is mostly hands-on, so robots come about 3 years after the thinking AI. What does that gap do for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me three years where St Brigid's office is all AI and I'm still at the bedside. I'd use them to make my name with families, so they ask for me by name. People will pay for a person they trust at the end of life, if they can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd have a baby sooner. Isn't that a risk if both your jobs are under threat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but my mum always says there's never a good time. I'd rather have a child while we've got two wages and a flat. Waiting for the world to calm down could mean waiting forever.

say: I'd say some things don't go to a **machine**, and **dying** is one.
I'd sign a **parish petition** if one started.
think: The **washing and turning** could go to robots by 2031.
**Daniel's plumbing** being threatened too scares me more.
do: Build up **private families** from church who want a person.
Save about **half of Daniel's** earnings for a year.
Marry and **try for a baby** sooner, while both earning.
S2.quote: There are some things you don't hand to a machine, and dying is one of them.
fieldNote: Her biggest fear is **both incomes** being hit around 2031.
She'd use the gap to be **asked for by name**, a reputation robots lack.
Having a child sooner reflects her **family values** over caution.

steps.text: Build a list of private church families who want a human carer
Save half of Daniel's plumbing earnings for a year
Marry Daniel and try for a baby sooner while both earn

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years and then robots around 2034. That's a bit more breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, that end-of-life care should stay human, but I'd say it calmer. I'd tell the younger carers at St Brigid's to get a proper qualification while there's time. At church I'd say families should plan to be there for their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think five years is enough to make myself the person families ask for. If I get a proper palliative care certificate, I'd be the one the hospice or a family calls when it matters most. The basic care work would still go by 2034, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a palliative care certificate at the college, evenings, starting next year. I'd keep the private sits going and grow them slowly. Once the charity's AI rota and notes arrive around 2031, I'd learn them properly, because that's where the shifts will be posted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, but more in charge of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years, compared with the fast one, change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes whether I scramble or plan. In the fast one I'd be grabbing families from church; with five years I can get qualified first, then build a name. My partner Daniel says five years is the difference between bailing water and building a boat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the basic care would still go. Who would you worry about at St Brigid's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The day carers who only do washing and dressing, like my friend Josie. She's got two little ones and no qualifications past school. I'd push her to do the certificate with me.

say: I'd say **end-of-life care** should stay human, but calmly.
I'd tell younger carers to get a **proper qualification** now.
think: Five years lets me become the person **families ask for**.
The **basic care work** would still go by 2034.
do: Do an **evening palliative care** certificate starting next year.
Learn the charity's **AI rota** when it arrives around 2031.
feel: **Anxious**, but more in charge of it.
S3.quote: My partner Daniel says five years is the difference between bailing water and building a boat.
fieldNote: The extra time turns **scrambling into planning**, in her partner's words.
She'd bring her friend **Josie** along to the certificate.
She bets on **specialist trust** lasting longer than basic care.

steps.text: Take an evening palliative care certificate at the college next year
Grow the private night sits for families slowly
Learn the charity's AI rota and notes system around 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, then robots in 2039. I'd be nearly forty, with children by then, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so don't panic, but don't sleep on it either. At church I'd say what I always say, look after your own. I'd tell Sister Margaret to plan the charity's future now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years feels safe for me personally. I'd have my best years at the bedside, and by forty I'd want to be doing something with fewer nights anyway. The charity's money would worry me more than robots for most of that decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd marry Daniel next year and start a family in the normal way. I'd keep doing the sits and personal care, and help Daniel buy a second van so his plumbing grows. Retraining I'd leave for my thirties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. The charity is still the thing in the back of my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When the thinking AI arrives in 2036, what happens to the parts of your work that aren't hands-on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The care plans and the handover notes would go to the AI, and I'd be glad. It's an hour a shift I'd rather spend with the family. Then I'd have three years of only the bedside part before robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why help Daniel's business rather than your own?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because his work is the bigger earner in a decade like that, and a second van means a second plumber. My mum and dad built their restaurant one table at a time, and in our house we pull the same way.

say: I'd say there's time, so **don't panic** but don't sleep on it.
I'd urge my manager to **plan the charity's future** now.
think: Ten years feels **safe for me** personally.
The **charity's money** would worry me more than robots.
By forty I'd want work with **fewer nights** anyway.
do: **Marry Daniel** next year and start a family.
Keep doing the **sits and personal care**.
Help buy a **second van** for Daniel's plumbing.
feel: **Calm**, with the charity at the back of her mind.
S4.quote: My mum and dad built their restaurant one table at a time, and in our house we pull the same way.
fieldNote: A decade lets her follow the **normal family path** she values.
She'd put money into **her partner's business**, as her parents did together.
Her lasting worry is **charity funding**, the same as in AI Plateau.

steps.text: Marry Daniel next year and start a family
Keep doing night sits and personal care at the charity
Help pay for a second van for Daniel's plumbing business

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Daniel's work and mine could both be hit around the same time, just when we'd want children. What would help is the government making sure families can still choose a person at the end of life, and that charities like St Brigid's get funding to keep us. Not handouts, just the work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the families, not just the carers. When someone's dying, the family needs a person in the room too, to make tea and say it's all right to sleep. A robot can turn a dying man, but it can't tell his daughter it's all right to go to bed.

headlineQuote: A robot can turn a dying man, but it can't tell his daughter it's all right to go to bed.
portrait: Kira is a **27-year-old end-of-life carer** at a charity in a seaside town, doing personal care and night sits.
Night sits pay well and her **parents helped buy** the flat she shares with Daniel, a plumber.
Her steady worry is the **charity's funding**, which matters more to her than AI in the slower pictures.
Fast AGI makes her build **private church clients** and start a family sooner; five years means a palliative certificate.
She believes a **trusted person** should be in the room at the end of life.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with her work and Daniel's hit around the same time.
whatWouldHelp: Families keeping the **choice of a person** at the end of life.
**Funding for charities** like St Brigid's to keep carers employed.
